title: Japan exits negative rates while retaining a buyer for government bonds
summary: On 19 March 2024 the Bank of Japan put the overnight call rate back at the centre of monetary policy. It judged that wages and domestic prices were reinforcing each other strongly enough to bring sustained 2% inflation into view toward the end of the January outlook’s projection period. That was a judgment about the durability of inflation. The Bank still expected accommodative financial conditions for the time being. It announced no timetable for another rate rise. The decision also judged the condition attached to its earlier inflation-overshooting commitment on the monetary base to have been fulfilled (p. 1 and footnote 1).

The Board voted 7–2 to guide the uncollateralized overnight call rate to roughly 0–0.1%. From 21 March the Bank would pay 0.1% on financial institutions’ current account balances excluding required reserves. The date matters for a daily time series. A market quote could respond at publication on 19 March, while the new remuneration and overnight operating guideline first applied two days later. The call-rate range and the rate paid on balances also describe different things. The former concerns overnight transactions among market participants, the latter a price offered on eligible balances at the central bank (p. 1 and footnote 2).

Ending yield curve control removed the explicit long-yield objective. Yet the Bank retained substantial discretion to buy government bonds. Purchases would initially continue at broadly their previous amount, then approximately ¥6 trillion per month. The Bank would announce purchase ranges and take market conditions and the supply and demand for JGBs into account. A rapid rise in long yields could elicit additional buying, fixed-rate purchase operations outside the monthly schedule, or funds supplied against pooled collateral. Traders therefore faced a different question from the one under an announced yield target. How large or abrupt would a rise have to be before the Bank intervened? No numerical threshold was supplied. The 8–1 vote on bond purchases also differed from the short-rate vote (p. 2 and footnote 3).

The treatment of other assets shows why a single balance-sheet variable gives a poor account of the exit. Purchases of equity exchange-traded funds and real-estate investment trusts would stop. Commercial paper and corporate bond purchases would decline gradually and end in about a year. The statement specified purchase policy without announcing sales of the accumulated stock. New loans under the lending stimulus, disaster-area and climate-finance operations would carry a 0.1% rate and one-year maturity. For the lending stimulus, a counterparty’s borrowing limit would equal its net increase in outstanding loans. These measures each passed unanimously. Equities, corporate credit, bank funding and government debt faced different changes in the terms or availability of official support (p. 2).

The evidence for the decision was more specific than the latest CPI reading. Corporate profits had improved and labour markets were tight. Initial spring wage negotiation results pointed to another year of firm wage gains. Contacts across the Bank’s head office and branches suggested that a broad range of firms intended to increase pay. Services prices were already rising moderately as the influence of earlier import-price increases faded. CPI excluding fresh food was around 2%, with government measures contributing to a substantial negative energy component. The Board expected that measure to exceed 2% through fiscal 2024 before slowing as temporary effects faded. At the same time it expected underlying inflation to rise as the output gap turned positive and wages and expectations increased. Those paths can coexist because they describe different components and horizons (pp. 2–4).

The dissent identified two ways the majority could be early. Toyoaki Nakamura wanted stronger evidence that smaller firms could afford higher pay after their lagging profit recovery. He nevertheless supported ending ETF purchases. Asahi Noguchi opposed ending negative rates and yield curve control together, citing uncertainty about the wage-price cycle and the risk of a discontinuous shift in financing conditions. He supported the bond-purchase guideline. The first objection points an analyst toward the distribution of operating profits, wages and pricing power across firms. The second points toward market liquidity and how quickly long and short borrowing costs adjusted to multiple changes on the same date (p. 3, notes 1–2).

The announcement arrived at 12:35 Japan time, seven minutes after the meeting ended. An event study can measure the change in overnight-indexed swaps, the government curve and the yen at that timestamp, then compare those changes with market expectations immediately beforehand. The policy itself moved in a tightening direction at the short end. The sign of a market surprise is a separate empirical result: participants might already have expected this decision and might instead revise their view of the next move or of the willingness to absorb bond supply. Neither the published general assessment of accommodative conditions nor an end-of-day yen move isolates those channels (pp. 1–2 and release reference).

questions.question: How much of the exit was already priced?
questions.detail: Capture the expected near-term overnight rate immediately before 12:35 Japan time. Compare its repricing with moves in forwards covering subsequent meetings and with the yen over identical windows. A limited response at the first meeting horizon alongside a larger shift further out would direct attention to expected follow-up policy. Timestamp wage news and press remarks separately.

questions.question: Did the continuing JGB purchase programme moderate long-yield volatility?
questions.detail: Overlay maturity-specific purchases and unscheduled operations on the ten- and thirty-year curves, swap spreads, bid–ask spreads and intraday volatility. Identify stress before an operation as well as conditions afterward. Since the Bank could buy in response to a spike, a simple correlation between larger purchases and higher volatility could reverse the direction of influence.

questions.question: Did wage gains become affordable at smaller firms?
questions.detail: Track wage settlements, realized base pay, operating margins and services prices by firm size and sector across successive releases. Compare firms with differing dependence on imported inputs and differing ability to pass costs on to customers. A wide gap between negotiated pay at large firms and realized pay at smaller employers would give Nakamura’s objection continuing relevance.

questions.question: Which prices absorbed the withdrawal of non-sovereign purchases?
questions.detail: For commercial paper and corporate bonds, compare financing spreads by maturity, credit quality and eligibility as purchase volumes fell. For equities and real estate, distinguish the end of new purchases from any later announcement about holdings. Keep the policy announcement distinct from the first subsequent operation and compare simultaneous moves in rates, exchange rates and broad risk assets.
